Enumeration literal for the HTTP GET method used in shoppingMall access logs.

This value represents read-only HTTP requests where clients retrieve resources such as catalog data, order details, or analytics views without modifying server state.

In reporting and analytics contexts, GET is often used to understand read traffic volume, cache effectiveness, and general browsing behaviour across different actor types and route patterns.

Enumeration literal for the HTTP POST method used in shoppingMall access logs.

This value represents write or creation operations in which clients submit data that usually results in new resources being created or workflows being triggered, such as placing orders, submitting reviews, or initiating authentication flows.

In analytics and observability use cases, POST is a key dimension for tracking business transactions, conversion funnels, and error rates for state-changing endpoints.

Enumeration literal for the HTTP PUT method used in shoppingMall access logs.

This value is associated with idempotent update operations where a client replaces or updates the full state of a resource, such as updating configuration entries, region settings, or other administrative records.

From a monitoring perspective, PUT calls help distinguish full-update traffic from partial updates and creations, allowing more precise error and performance analysis for administrative and operational APIs.

Enumeration literal for the HTTP PATCH method used in shoppingMall access logs.

This value corresponds to partial update operations where only subsets of a resource are changed, such as editing selected fields of a product, order, or policy configuration without replacing the entire object.

In analytics and dashboard views, PATCH traffic is useful to track fine-grained maintenance activity, incremental changes to catalog and policy data, and to separate those from full updates and creations.

Enumeration literal for the HTTP DELETE method stored in shoppingMall access logs.

This value captures destructive or deactivation operations where resources such as products, carts, or configuration rows are removed or logically retired from active use.

In operational analytics, DELETE calls are important for understanding data lifecycle patterns, cleanup behaviours, and potential risk areas where accidental or malicious deletions may occur.

Enumeration literal for the HTTP OPTIONS method recorded in shoppingMall access logs.

This value primarily appears in preflight requests, especially for CORS scenarios where the client discovers allowed methods, headers, and credentials for a target route before sending the actual business request.

While OPTIONS does not typically represent business activity, it is useful in traffic analytics and troubleshooting cross-origin issues, as well as understanding how often browsers probe specific endpoints.

Enumeration literal for the HTTP HEAD method tracked in shoppingMall access logs.

This value represents requests where the client retrieves response headers and metadata without the response body, which can be used for health checks, cache validation, or lightweight resource existence checks.

In observability and analytics, HEAD traffic helps identify monitoring and infrastructure-level probes separately from full content retrieval via GET.

IEShoppingMallHttpMethod.description:
Enumeration of HTTP methods that the shoppingMall backend records in its access logging and analytics tables.

This type is used by logging, analytics, and reporting DTOs to represent the HTTP method dimension in a strongly typed way, for example when aggregating traffic by method, computing error rates per verb, or segmenting dashboards by read versus write operations.

The set of values is intentionally limited to the HTTP methods that are relevant and expected in the public and administrative APIs of the shoppingMall platform: the common REST verbs GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, and DELETE, plus OPTIONS and HEAD for preflight and metadata-only requests. Methods such as TRACE or CONNECT are not included because they are not exposed or tracked as part of normal business API traffic within this system.

oneOf.description:
Enumeration literal for the 1xx informational HTTP status code family.

This bucket represents provisional responses such as 100 Continue and 101 Switching Protocols that may be observed at the edge or in infrastructure components.

In most business-facing analytics for the shoppingMall platform this family is rare, but it is included for completeness when analysing low-level access logs or unusual integration behaviours.

Enumeration literal for the 2xx success HTTP status code family.

This family includes codes such as 200 OK, 201 Created, and 204 No Content that indicate successful handling of client requests at the application level.

In operational and business analytics, 2xx responses represent successful transactions, completed API calls, and healthy behaviour. Ratios of 2xx responses compared to other families are a primary signal for service reliability and customer experience.

Enumeration literal for the 3xx redirection HTTP status code family.

This family comprises response codes such as 301 Moved Permanently and 302 Found, which instruct clients to repeat the request at a different URI or follow another navigation path.

When used in shoppingMall analytics, 3xx responses help identify redirection patterns, routing behaviours, and potential misconfigurations in URL structures or external integration flows.

Enumeration literal for the 4xx client error HTTP status code family.

This bucket covers codes such as 400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized, 403 Forbidden, and 404 Not Found, which generally indicate that the request was invalid, unauthenticated, unauthorized, or targeted a non-existent resource.

Dashboards and reports commonly use the 4xx family to monitor client-side integration issues, validation failures, authentication problems, and routing mistakes, enabling platform operators to distinguish client-side faults from server-side failures.

Enumeration literal for the 5xx server error HTTP status code family.

This family includes codes such as 500 Internal Server Error, 502 Bad Gateway, and 503 Service Unavailable that signal failures within the server, backend dependencies, or infrastructure.

In the shoppingMall platform, 5xx responses are a critical signal for reliability and incident management. Aggregating metrics by this family allows operators to quickly identify degradation, track incident impact, and prioritise remediation efforts separately from client-side or redirection-related behaviours.

IEShoppingMallStatusCodeFamily.description:
Enumeration of coarse-grained HTTP status code families derived from raw numeric status codes in shoppingMall logging and analytics tables.

Instead of tracking every individual HTTP status code in high-level dashboards and reports, the platform often aggregates results into these five standard families: informational 1xx, successful 2xx, redirection 3xx, client error 4xx, and server error 5xx. This provides a concise but expressive view of service health and error patterns.

This type is used by log-based analytics, observability DTOs, and reporting endpoints to express status distributions, error breakdowns, and time-series trends. By working with status code families, operators and analysts can quickly understand the balance between successful traffic and different classes of issues without being overwhelmed by fine-grained code-level detail.

IShoppingMallAuthenticationFailureReason.description: Aggregated statistics for a single authentication failure reason over a given analysis window.

reasonCode.description: Machine-readable reason code for the authentication failure category (for example, `INVALID_CREDENTIALS`, `ACCOUNT_LOCKED`, `POLICY_VIOLATION`).

label.description: Human-readable label for the failure reason, suitable for display in admin dashboards.

count.description: Total number of authentication failures attributed to this reason within the selected time range.

IShoppingMallAuthenticationActorTypeSumm.description: Aggregated authentication statistics for a single actor type over a given analysis window.

actorType.description: Actor classification for which these metrics are computed (for example, customer, seller, platformAdmin, guestUser).

totalAttempts.description: Total number of authentication attempts (successful and failed) performed by this actor type during the analysis window.

successfulAttempts.description: Number of successful authentication attempts for this actor type during the analysis window.

failedAttempts.description: Number of failed authentication attempts for this actor type during the analysis window.

IShoppingMallAuthenticationTimeBucketSum.description:
Time-bucketed authentication metrics for a specific time slice within a broader authentication analytics window.

This schema represents an aggregated view derived from raw authentication and session events, grouped into a single contiguous time bucket. It is typically used by dashboards, monitoring pipelines, and anomaly detection services to visualize how authentication activity evolves over time and to compare neighboring buckets for spikes or drops.

Each instance of this type covers a half-open time interval expressed in UTC using ISO 8601 `date-time` strings. The bucket boundaries are determined by the analytics granularity (for example, minute, hour, day), and the counters represent already-aggregated counts for that exact interval rather than individual log records.

bucketStartAt.description:
Inclusive start instant of this time bucket in ISO 8601 `date-time` format, always expressed in UTC.

`bucketStartAt` marks the exact timestamp at which this bucket begins. All authentication events whose timestamps are greater than or equal to this value and strictly less than `bucketEndAt` are considered part of this bucket for aggregation.

The value is typically aligned to the chosen analytics granularity (for example, the start of the minute or hour) so that adjacent buckets partition the overall analysis window without gaps or overlaps.

bucketEndAt.description:
Exclusive end instant of this time bucket in ISO 8601 `date-time` format, always expressed in UTC.

`bucketEndAt` marks the upper bound of the half-open interval `[bucketStartAt, bucketEndAt)`. Authentication events whose timestamps are greater than or equal to `bucketStartAt` but strictly earlier than this value are included in the bucket; events at or after `bucketEndAt` are counted in subsequent buckets.

The difference between `bucketEndAt` and `bucketStartAt` corresponds to the analytics bucket size (for example, one minute, five minutes, one hour), and adjacent buckets are expected to share boundaries without gaps.

totalLoginAttempts.description:
Total number of authentication attempts observed within this time bucket after any filtering or preprocessing applied by the analytics pipeline.

In a typical configuration, this count should be equal to the sum of `successfulLoginAttempts` and `failedLoginAttempts`. If these values diverge, it usually indicates partial ingestion, additional filtering applied to certain outcomes, or advanced classification where some events are excluded from success/failure tallies.

This metric is commonly used to measure overall authentication throughput and to normalize success or failure ratios when comparing multiple time buckets.

successfulLoginAttempts.description:
Number of successful authentication attempts within this time bucket.

This counter includes events that passed all authentication checks (for example, credential validation and any configured multi-factor challenges) and resulted in an established session or token. It is a derived, aggregate metric meant for analytics, not a direct count of underlying log rows.

Operators and analytics tools use this value together with `failedLoginAttempts` and `totalLoginAttempts` to compute success rates, detect sudden drops in successful logins, and distinguish between genuine traffic growth and abnormal failure spikes.

failedLoginAttempts.description:
Number of failed authentication attempts within this time bucket.

This count includes authentication attempts that were rejected for reasons such as invalid credentials, expired accounts, failed multi-factor checks, or policy violations. It is derived from the underlying authentication logs and may exclude certain internal or test traffic depending on the implementation.

A rising trend in `failedLoginAttempts`, especially when paired with stable or decreasing `successfulLoginAttempts`, can be an indicator of credential stuffing, brute-force attempts, or misconfiguration and is often used as an input to anomaly detection and alerting logic.

IShoppingMallAuthenticationAnomalyIndica.description:
Represents a detected anomaly in authentication activity for a given analysis window.

Anomalies may include sudden spikes in failed logins, unusually high activity from a small set of IP ranges, deviations from baseline success ratios, or other patterns that suggest abuse, misconfiguration, or degraded user experience.

Detection strategies are implementation-specific and may rely on statistical thresholds, rule-based heuristics, or external risk engines, and they can evolve over time without changing the structure of this DTO. This type is typically returned alongside time-bucketed authentication metrics or higher-level security analytics to guide operators toward buckets or segments that deserve closer investigation.

code.description:
Stable, machine-readable anomaly code that classifies the type of authentication anomaly (for example, `FAILURE_SPIKE`, `SUSPICIOUS_IP_ACTIVITY`, `UNUSUAL_GEO_DISTRIBUTION`).

The code is intended for use in dashboards, filters, alert routing rules, and analytics queries. It should follow a consistent naming convention (commonly upper‑snake‑case) and be treated as part of the public contract: once introduced, a code should not be renamed casually because external consumers may rely on it for automation and reporting.

Implementations may define a finite catalog of supported codes and evolve that catalog over time as new detection patterns are introduced.

oneOf.description:
Low-severity informational anomaly used primarily for visibility, tuning, and trend analysis rather than immediate operational action.

`info` anomalies highlight unusual but not inherently dangerous authentication patterns, such as minor deviations from baseline during known marketing campaigns or seasonal traffic shifts. They are useful for analysts and engineers monitoring system behavior but typically do not trigger tickets or pager alerts on their own.

Medium-severity anomaly that suggests noteworthy or potentially risky authentication behavior which warrants manual review.

`warning` anomalies might include elevated failure rates from a specific region, repeated attempts against a small set of accounts, or patterns that could represent early stages of abuse. They are suitable for non-paging alerts, ticket creation, or inclusion in daily security and operations review reports.

High-severity anomaly that strongly indicates active abuse, compromise attempts, or severe misconfiguration in authentication flows.

`critical` anomalies represent patterns such as extreme failure spikes resembling credential stuffing, high-volume attacks from known bad IP ranges, or behavior that maps to incident playbooks. They should typically feed into paging, incident management workflows, or immediate security response processes.

severity.description:
Severity level of the anomaly as assessed by the detection logic.

Severity controls how anomalies are visualized in dashboards, how they are routed through alerting systems, and how urgently operators are expected to respond. Implementations should apply consistent criteria when assigning severities so that `info`, `warning`, and `critical` anomalies have predictable operational meaning across the platform.

Clients can use severity to filter, sort, and prioritize anomalies when building security overviews, incident queues, or health dashboards.

message.description:
Human-readable description of the anomaly suitable for admin dashboards, security teams, and alerting systems.

The message should concisely summarize what was detected and, when possible, include actionable context such as affected regions, time windows, or actor types (for example, “Spike in failed customer logins from Region EU within the last 15 minutes”). It should remain short enough to display comfortably in lists and notification channels.

To protect privacy and security, the message must not include secret credentials or directly identifying personal data such as full email addresses or IP lists. Instead, it should refer to higher-level aggregates or anonymized identifiers while still providing enough detail for an operator to decide on appropriate follow-up actions.

IShoppingMallErrorSummary.description:
Aggregated error analytics summary derived from the shopping_mall_error_logs table.

Represents precomputed monitoring and troubleshooting metrics instead of raw log rows. Intended for admin dashboards and operational tools rather than direct log exploration.

buckets.description:
Collection of aggregated error metric buckets, typically grouped by time window and/or error category.

Each bucket contains counts, rates, and optional distribution details for a specific dimension such as time interval, HTTP status family, route, or error category.

totalErrorCount.description: Total number of error log entries matching the applied filters across the entire requested interval.

uniqueErrorSignatures.description:
Number of distinct error signatures or unique error keys observed in the filtered data set.

This is commonly computed from a normalized error fingerprint, such as a hash of message and stack trace.

errorRatePerMinute.description: Average error rate per minute over the requested time range, computed as totalErrorCount divided by the number of minutes in the interval.

from.description:
Start of the time range actually used for aggregation, in ISO 8601 date-time format.

May be adjusted by the backend if the requested range is partially outside stored data retention.

to.description:
End of the time range actually used for aggregation, in ISO 8601 date-time format.

May be adjusted by the backend if the requested range is partially outside stored data retention.

IShoppingMallErrorSummary.IRequest.description:
Filter and aggregation criteria for computing error analytics over the shopping_mall_error_logs table.

This DTO allows platform administrators to define which subset of error logs to analyze and how to group the resulting metrics. It includes a required time range and optional filters for routes, services, severity levels, error categories, environments, and time-bucket granularity.

All fields are used exclusively for read-only analytical queries; this request does not create, modify, or delete any error log records.

timeRange.description:
Time window to analyze in the error logs.

Implementations should enforce a valid range (for example, ensuring start precedes end and the duration does not exceed configured limits).

oneOf.description:
Optional list of API route prefixes or patterns whose errors should be included in the analysis.

Examples: "/shoppingMall/orders", "/shoppingMall/payments", "/shoppingMall/platformAdmin". If omitted or empty, errors from all routes are included.

routePrefixes.description:
Optional list of API route prefixes or patterns whose errors should be included in the analysis.

Examples: "/shoppingMall/orders", "/shoppingMall/payments", "/shoppingMall/platformAdmin". If omitted or empty, errors from all routes are included.

oneOf.description:
Optional list of logical service or subsystem identifiers recorded in error logs.

These identifiers allow operators to restrict analytics to specific bounded contexts or microservices if such metadata is present in shopping_mall_error_logs.

services.description:
Optional list of logical service or subsystem identifiers recorded in error logs.

These identifiers allow operators to restrict analytics to specific bounded contexts or microservices if such metadata is present in shopping_mall_error_logs.

items.description: Severity level label such as DEBUG, INFO, WARN, ERROR, or FATAL, depending on the logging configuration.

oneOf.description:
Optional list of severity levels to include in the analysis.

If omitted or empty, errors of all severities are included.

severityLevels.description:
Optional list of severity levels to include in the analysis.

If omitted or empty, errors of all severities are included.

items.description: Application-specific error category label such as VALIDATION_ERROR, AUTHENTICATION_ERROR, BUSINESS_RULE_VIOLATION, or INFRASTRUCTURE_FAILURE.

oneOf.description:
Optional list of application-specific error categories to include in the analysis.

If omitted or empty, errors from all categories are included.

errorCategories.description:
Optional list of application-specific error categories to include in the analysis.

If omitted or empty, errors from all categories are included.

items.description: Environment label recorded with error logs, such as "production", "staging", or "development".

oneOf.description:
Optional list of environment identifiers to filter the analysis (for example, production-only vs staging-only).

If omitted or empty, errors from all environments are included.

environments.description:
Optional list of environment identifiers to filter the analysis (for example, production-only vs staging-only).

If omitted or empty, errors from all environments are included.

timeBucket.description:
Requested time-bucket granularity for the errorsOverTime series.

As with access traffic analytics, implementations may adjust or cap the bucket size based on the requested time range to balance detail with payload size.

oneOf.description:
Represents a one‑minute time-bucket granularity for analytics time series in the ShoppingMall platform.

This option provides the highest temporal resolution and is best suited for very short analysis windows, such as active incident debugging or verification of a recent deployment. When used over long time ranges, it can produce a very large number of buckets and high-volume response payloads, which may impact dashboard rendering and query performance.

Platform operators should typically reserve this granularity for focused troubleshooting sessions or automated tools that explicitly need per-minute visibility into error or traffic behavior.

Represents a five‑minute time-bucket granularity for analytics time series in the ShoppingMall platform.

This option offers a balance between fine-grained visibility and practical bucket counts. It is well-suited for short to medium analysis windows, such as monitoring the last few hours of activity during a rollout, investigating transient error spikes, or powering near real‑time operational dashboards.

Compared to per-minute buckets, five‑minute buckets reduce noise and payload size while still allowing operators to locate narrow windows of degraded behavior with reasonable precision.

Represents a fifteen‑minute time-bucket granularity for analytics time series in the ShoppingMall platform.

This option is a strong default for many operational monitoring scenarios where the analysis window spans several hours up to a couple of days. It smooths out very short-lived fluctuations to highlight meaningful trends while keeping the number of buckets and response payload size manageable.

Use this granularity for standard admin dashboards, daily reliability reviews, or when analyzing error and traffic patterns around business events without needing per‑minute detail.

Represents an hourly time-bucket granularity for analytics time series in the ShoppingMall platform.

Hourly buckets are appropriate when examining behavior across longer windows, such as full days or multiple days, where per-minute or five‑minute detail would create an excessive number of buckets. This granularity is effective for understanding diurnal patterns, evaluating the impact of planned maintenance, and performing coarse-grained trend analysis.

Because each bucket aggregates an hour of activity, brief spikes may be partially smoothed, but major incidents and sustained periods of elevated errors remain clearly visible.

Represents a daily time-bucket granularity for analytics time series in the ShoppingMall platform.

This option is designed for long-term historical analysis, such as weekly, monthly, or quarterly reporting on reliability, traffic, or integration health. It dramatically reduces the number of buckets across large time ranges, making it suitable for management reports, SLA reviews, and capacity planning views.

Operators should be aware that short-lived incidents can be smoothed within a daily bucket. Daily granularity is therefore best used in combination with higher-resolution analyses when a particular period of interest is identified.

IShoppingMallAnalyticsTimeBucketOption.description:
Standardized time-bucket granularity selector used by ShoppingMall analytics endpoints when generating time-series metrics.

Smaller bucket sizes (such as `minute` or `fiveMinutes`) provide higher temporal resolution and are appropriate for short analysis windows and detailed incident investigations, but they increase the number of buckets, response payload size, and query cost. Larger bucket sizes (such as `hour` or `day`) aggregate more data into each bucket, which improves performance and readability for long-term trend analysis, historical reporting, and management dashboards at the expense of fine-grained detail.

Callers should choose the smallest bucket size that still keeps the bucket count and payload size reasonable for the requested time range and the intended use case of the analytics output.

IShoppingMallAccessTrafficSummaryByHttpM.description:
Access traffic metrics grouped by HTTP method for a given analysis window.

This DTO represents a single bucket in HTTP method based access analytics. Each instance aggregates the number of requests that were observed with a particular HTTP method (for example, GET, POST, PATCH, PUT, or DELETE) over a defined time window or filter scope.

It is typically used inside higher‑level access analytics responses such as IShoppingMallAccessTrafficSummary, allowing dashboards and reporting tools to quickly render method distribution charts without re‑computing raw log data.

httpMethod.description:
HTTP method for this traffic bucket.

This field is constrained to the shared platform enum `IEShoppingMallHttpMethod`, which represents the normalized set of HTTP methods that the shoppingMall access logging layer records (for example, GET, POST, PATCH, PUT, DELETE).

Using the enum instead of a free‑form string guarantees type‑safe grouping and consistent analytics across all logging and metrics DTOs.

requestCount.description:
Number of requests recorded with this HTTP method within the analysis window.

This value is an aggregated count derived from the access log table (shopping_mall_access_logs) after applying the caller’s filters such as time range, actor type, or route pattern.

It is always a non‑negative integer and is intended for use in dashboards, summaries, and alerts that visualize traffic distribution by HTTP method.

IShoppingMallAccessTrafficSummaryByStatu.description:
Access traffic metrics grouped by HTTP status code family for a given analysis window.

This DTO represents a single bucket in status code family based access analytics. Each instance aggregates the number of requests whose responses fall into a particular HTTP status code family (for example, 2xx, 3xx, 4xx, or 5xx) according to the normalized enum used across the platform.

It is usually consumed as part of higher‑level access or error analytics responses to render response health charts and error‑rate distributions without scanning raw log rows.

statusCodeFamily.description:
HTTP status code family identifier for this traffic bucket.

This field is constrained to the shared enum `IEShoppingMallStatusCodeFamily`, which represents canonical families such as "2xx", "3xx", "4xx", and "5xx" used consistently across error and access analytics DTOs.

Using a common enum ensures that status‑family based grouping is type‑safe, avoids typos, and stays aligned with other logging and monitoring components.

requestCount.description:
Number of requests whose response status falls into this status code family within the analysis window.

This value is computed from the access log data (shopping_mall_access_logs) after applying the caller’s filters such as time range, actor type, or route pattern.

It is always a non‑negative integer, and is typically visualized to monitor the proportion of successful, redirected, client‑error, and server‑error responses over time.

IShoppingMallAccessTrafficSummaryByRoute.description:
Access traffic metrics grouped by canonical route pattern for a given analysis window.

This DTO represents a single aggregation bucket keyed by a normalized route pattern derived from `shopping_mall_access_logs`. Each instance summarizes how many requests hit a specific logical endpoint, with dynamic path parameters normalized into template placeholders so that different concrete URLs are counted together.

It is primarily used by observability and analytics features such as admin dashboards, traffic hotspot analysis, capacity planning, and routing optimization, where operators need to understand which functional areas of the ShoppingMall HTTP API receive the most traffic over a selected time window.

routePattern.description:
Canonical route pattern or route identifier used to group access logs.

Dynamic path parameters are normalized into template placeholders so that concrete URLs are grouped into a single logical bucket. For example, requests to `/shoppingMall/orders/123` and `/shoppingMall/orders/456` would typically be normalized to a pattern such as `/shoppingMall/orders/{orderId}`.

The exact normalization rules should mirror the routing configuration and the way `shopping_mall_access_logs` stores or derives route information, ensuring stable analytics over time even as individual resource IDs change.

requestCount.description:
Number of requests that matched this route pattern within the analysis window.

The value is a non‑negative, aggregated counter computed from `shopping_mall_access_logs` over the caller-specified time range and filter set, not a field stored directly on any single log record. A value of `0` indicates no matching traffic for the pattern, while larger values highlight heavily used endpoints.

This metric is typically used in dashboards and reports to identify high-traffic routes, detect potential bottlenecks, and drive capacity planning or API design optimizations.

IShoppingMallAccessTrafficSummaryByActor.description:
Access traffic metrics grouped by actor type for a given analysis window.

Each instance represents a single aggregation bucket corresponding to a logical actor classification (for example, guest visitor, authenticated customer, seller, or platform administrator). The underlying data is derived from `shopping_mall_access_logs` combined with authentication and session context to determine which actor type initiated each request.

These summaries are used in security, product, and UX analytics to compare how different actor segments interact with the platform, monitor anomalous activity patterns, and inform capacity planning or feature prioritization for specific user groups.

actorType.description:
Actor type label representing the kind of identity associated with the request.

Typical values include logical labels such as `guest`, `customer`, `seller`, and `platformAdmin`, corresponding to unauthenticated visitors, end customers, marketplace sellers, and platform administrators respectively. Anonymous or unauthenticated traffic should be grouped under a consistent label such as `guest` so that it can be analyzed separately from authenticated activity.

The exact set of supported labels should align with the actor classifications used by the authentication, session, and logging subsystems, ensuring that access traffic analytics and security monitoring dashboards present a coherent view across the platform.

requestCount.description:
Number of requests issued by this actor type within the analysis window.

The value is a non‑negative, aggregated counter computed from `shopping_mall_access_logs` after grouping requests by actor classification, rather than a field stored directly on any single record. It reflects the total volume of traffic generated by the actor segment for the chosen time range and any additional filters applied.

This metric is commonly used to compare engagement between guests and authenticated users, monitor seller and admin activity, and detect unusual spikes that may indicate abuse, misconfiguration, or unexpected usage patterns.

IShoppingMallAccessTrafficSummaryTimeBuc.description:
Time-bucketed access traffic metrics for a single contiguous time slice within a larger analysis window.

Each instance of this type represents one bucket in a time series that summarizes HTTP access traffic derived from the `shopping_mall_access_logs` table. Buckets are aligned to the time-bucket granularity selected in the parent `IShoppingMallAccessTrafficSummary.IRequest` (for example minute, hour, or day).

All counts in this structure are calculated **after** the server has applied every filter specified in the parent request, such as actor type, HTTP method, status-code family, and route pattern. As a result, clients can safely treat each bucket as an already-filtered view of traffic for visualization and analytics purposes.

bucketStart.description:
Start timestamp of the time bucket in ISO 8601 `date-time` format (UTC).

This value represents the **inclusive lower bound** of the bucket. It is aligned to the configured analytics granularity (for example, the start of the minute, hour, or day) and always falls within the overall analysis window requested by the client.

When aggregating records from `shopping_mall_access_logs`, any log entry with a timestamp greater than or equal to `bucketStart` and strictly less than `bucketEnd` will be counted in this bucket.

bucketEnd.description:
End timestamp of the time bucket in ISO 8601 `date-time` format (UTC).

This value represents the **exclusive upper bound** of the bucket. In a typical series it is equal to `bucketStart` plus one unit of the selected time-bucket duration (for example, one minute, one hour, or one day). Records with timestamps in the half-open interval `[bucketStart, bucketEnd)` belong to this bucket.

For the last bucket in an analysis window, `bucketEnd` may be equal to the overall analysis end time even if the bucket does not represent a full period, allowing partially filled trailing buckets to be returned in a consistent way.

requestCount.description:
Number of access log entries observed within this time bucket after all analytics filters have been applied.

The server computes this value from the `shopping_mall_access_logs` table by counting log records whose timestamps fall within `[bucketStart, bucketEnd)` and that match every filter provided in `IShoppingMallAccessTrafficSummary.IRequest` (such as actor type, HTTP method, status-code family, and route pattern).

Any internal de-duplication, exclusion of health checks, or bot filtering is performed before this aggregation step. Therefore, `requestCount` reflects the effective traffic level that should be presented to operators in dashboards, charts, or export reports.

IShoppingMallErrorSummary.IBucket.description:
Single aggregated error metrics bucket within an error analytics summary.

Represents metrics for a combination of dimensions such as time window, HTTP status family, route, or logical error category.

timeWindowStart.description:
Start timestamp of the time window represented by this bucket, in ISO 8601 date-time format.

Optional for non-time-based aggregations where grouping is purely categorical.

timeWindowEnd.description:
End timestamp of the time window represented by this bucket, in ISO 8601 date-time format.

Optional for non-time-based aggregations where grouping is purely categorical.

route.description:
Normalized API route or operation key associated with this bucket.

Commonly a pattern such as /orders or /products/{productId}, or an internal operation name. Can be omitted when grouping is not per-route.

service.description:
Logical service or subsystem name associated with this bucket.

Used to aggregate errors per microservice, module, or bounded context within the ShoppingMall backend.

statusFamily.description:
HTTP status code family represented by this bucket (for example, "4xx" or "5xx").

Not all aggregations include status grouping; omit this field when not applicable.

errorCategory.description:
High-level error category or classification key (for example, "validation", "auth", "db", or "integration").

Used to group similar failures under a common label.

errorCount.description: Number of error log entries falling into this bucket for the selected dimensions.

errorRate.description:
Error rate for this bucket over its time window, expressed as errors per minute or another backend-defined unit.

Exact semantics depend on how the aggregation query is implemented.

topErrorSignatures.description:
Optional list of the most frequent error signatures in this bucket, sorted by descending occurrence.

Each signature summarizes a recurring error pattern by key, example message, and count.

IShoppingMallErrorSummary.IErrorSignatur.description:
Summary of a recurring error signature within an error analytics bucket.

Represents a deduplicated error pattern derived from one or more error log rows, typically identified by hashing message and stack trace or by a normalized key.

signatureKey.description: Stable identifier for the error signature, such as a hash of normalized error message and stack trace or a domain-specific error code.

exampleMessage.description: Representative error message for this signature taken from one of the underlying error log entries.

occurrenceCount.description: Number of times this error signature appears within the aggregation scope for its parent bucket.

IShoppingMallIntegrationEventSummary.IRe.description:
Analytics query parameters for retrieving aggregated integration event log summaries.

This DTO allows platform administrators to define time ranges, filtering conditions, and aggregation preferences for computing summaries over the `shopping_mall_integration_event_logs` table. It is designed purely for read-only analytics queries and does not expose any fields that would mutate underlying log records.

from.description:
Start of the time range for which to compute integration event metrics, in ISO 8601 date-time format (UTC).

This timestamp is inclusive and typically required to avoid unbounded queries that could degrade performance.

to.description:
End of the time range for which to compute integration event metrics, in ISO 8601 date-time format (UTC).

This timestamp is exclusive and must be greater than the `from` value. The backend will validate that the requested interval is within acceptable limits.

integrationPartnerKeys.description:
Optional list of integration partner identifiers to include in the summary.

When provided, only events whose partner key matches one of the values in this array will be considered. When omitted or empty, events from all partners are included.

eventTypes.description:
Optional list of event types or categories to include in the summary.

This allows narrowing the aggregation to specific types of integration interactions such as webhooks, callbacks, or synchronization tasks. When omitted or empty, all event types are included.

statusGroups.description:
Optional list of high-level status groups to include in the summary.

Typical values include `SUCCESS`, `FAILURE`, or other platform-defined groupings. When omitted or empty, events from all status groups are included.

groupBy.description:
How to group events when building aggregation buckets.

Common values include `time`, `partner`, `eventType`, or composite options like `timeAndPartner`. The exact supported values are defined by the implementation and may be validated server-side.

timeGranularity.description:
Time granularity to use when `groupBy` includes a time dimension.

Common values are `hour`, `day`, or `week`. The backend uses this to determine how to bucket timestamps into time windows and may reject unsupported values.

limit.description:
Optional maximum number of metric buckets to return.

This acts as a safety control to prevent excessively large responses and to support UI scenarios such as "top N partners by error ratio". When omitted, the backend uses a sensible default limit.

includeLatencyPercentiles.description:
Whether to calculate and include latency percentile fields (p50, p90, p99) in each bucket.

Disabling this flag can reduce computation cost for coarse-grained monitoring where percentile details are not required.

IShoppingMallIntegrationEventSummary.description:
Aggregated analytics summary of integration event logs for external integrations in the shopping mall platform.

This DTO represents read-only, computed metrics over the immutable Prisma log table `shopping_mall_integration_event_logs`. It is used by platform administrators and SRE/operations tooling to understand how integration partners and infrastructure services are behaving over time, including event volumes, success and failure ratios, and latency distributions.

Each summary object typically corresponds to a time window and a particular grouping key such as integration partner identifier, event type, or overall platform aggregate, depending on the query configuration. The metrics are suitable for charting and dashboard visualization and never expose raw log payloads.

buckets.description:
List of aggregated metric buckets computed from integration event logs.

Each bucket represents a grouping such as a specific time window, integration partner, event type, or a combination of these, depending on the request. Buckets contain counts and latency statistics derived from many underlying `shopping_mall_integration_event_logs` records.

generatedAt.description:
Timestamp when this summary snapshot was generated on the server, in ISO 8601 date-time format (UTC).

Clients can use this to understand data freshness and to avoid mixing metrics from different calculation runs.

totalEvents.description:
Total number of integration events included in this summary across all buckets.

This is the sum of the event counts for all buckets after applying the filters from the request.

totalSuccesses.description:
Total number of successful integration events across all buckets.

A successful event usually corresponds to a status such as `SUCCESS` or similar in the underlying `shopping_mall_integration_event_logs` table.

totalFailures.description:
Total number of failed integration events across all buckets.

Failures include events with statuses such as `ERROR`, `TIMEOUT`, or any other non-success status stored in `shopping_mall_integration_event_logs`.

IShoppingMallIntegrationEventSummary.IBu.description:
Single analytics bucket representing aggregated metrics for a slice of integration event logs.

Buckets are computed by grouping log entries by time window, integration partner identifier, event type, status set, or combinations of these dimensions, depending on the query. Each bucket contains counts for total events and failures, as well as latency statistics suitable for plotting in dashboards.

windowStart.description:
Start timestamp of the time window for this bucket in ISO 8601 date-time format (UTC).

When the query groups by time (for example, per hour or per day), this marks the inclusive beginning of the interval represented by this bucket.

windowEnd.description:
End timestamp of the time window for this bucket in ISO 8601 date-time format (UTC).

When the query groups by time (for example, per hour or per day), this marks the exclusive end of the interval represented by this bucket.

integrationPartnerKey.description:
Identifier of the integration partner or external subsystem that this bucket is summarizing.

Typical values are stable keys or codes configured for external payment gateways, logistics providers, notification services, or internal infrastructure integrations. When the query does not group by partner, this field may be a generic key like `ALL` to indicate a global aggregate.

eventType.description:
Logical type or category of integration events summarized in this bucket.

Examples include `webhook`, `paymentCallback`, `shipmentUpdate`, or other domain-specific event categories used in `shopping_mall_integration_event_logs`. When the query does not group by event type, this field may be a generic key like `ALL`.

statusGroup.description:
High-level status grouping for the events in this bucket.

Common values are `SUCCESS`, `FAILURE`, or other platform-specific groupings that aggregate multiple low-level status codes from the underlying log table into broader categories used for analytics.

eventCount.description:
Total number of events in `shopping_mall_integration_event_logs` that fall into this bucket after filtering and grouping.

This includes both successful and failed events.

successCount.description:
Number of successful integration events in this bucket.

Success is determined based on status fields in the underlying log entries that correspond to normal, expected behavior.

failureCount.description:
Number of failed integration events in this bucket.

Failures include events with statuses such as errors, timeouts, or rejected responses from external partners.

errorRatio.description:
Error ratio for this bucket, represented as a floating-point value between 0 and 1.

It is typically computed as `failureCount / eventCount` when `eventCount` is greater than zero. When there are no events, implementations may set this to 0.

avgLatencyMs.description:
Average latency in milliseconds for integration events in this bucket.

Latency is usually measured as the time between when the integration call was initiated and when a response or timeout occurred.

p50LatencyMs.description:
50th percentile (median) latency in milliseconds for events in this bucket.

Helps understand typical integration response times beyond the average.

p90LatencyMs.description:
90th percentile latency in milliseconds for events in this bucket.

Highlights slower responses affecting a minority of events.

p99LatencyMs.description:
99th percentile latency in milliseconds for events in this bucket.

Useful for identifying extreme outliers and tail latency behavior.

IShoppingMallSecurityIncidentReport.description:
Security incident report response for platform administrators.

Represents a paginated, aggregated view of security-related incidents derived from system-generated logging tables such as shopping_mall_security_events, shopping_mall_auth_logs, and shopping_mall_access_logs. Each report contains pagination metadata and a collection of incident summaries that security and operations teams can review, filter, and export for incident response and compliance.

pagination.description: Pagination information for the security incident report result set, including current page, page size, total items, and navigation cursors or offsets.

data.description: Array of security incident summaries matching the specified search and filter criteria. Each element represents a single security-relevant incident derived from one or more underlying log records.

IShoppingMallSecurityIncidentSummary.description:
Summary view of a single security incident derived from security and authentication logging tables.

Each summary aggregates key data points from shopping_mall_security_events, shopping_mall_auth_logs, shopping_mall_access_logs, or related logging models to describe one security-relevant incident for quick review in lists and dashboards.

id.description: Stable identifier of the security incident within the reporting subsystem. This may be a synthetic identifier that groups one or more underlying log records into a single incident.

occurredAt.description: Timestamp when this security incident was detected or considered to have occurred. Uses ISO 8601 date-time format in UTC.

category.description: High-level category that classifies the incident type, such as authenticationAnomaly, accessPolicyViolation, suspectedFraud, or integrationSecurityIssue.

severity.description: Severity level assigned to this incident based on detection rules or risk assessment. Typical values include info, warning, and critical.

summary.description: Short human-readable description of the incident for quick scanning in list views and dashboards.

principalType.description: Type of actor associated with this incident, if any. Indicates whether the incident relates to a customer, seller, platform administrator, or an anonymous/guest context.

principalId.description: Identifier of the principal associated with this incident when available. May reference a customer, seller, or platform admin account, or be null when the incident is not tied to a specific identity.

ipAddress.description: Source IP address associated with the incident, if captured by logging. Useful for correlation and threat hunting workflows.

sessionId.description: Session identifier associated with the incident when available, typically referencing a customer, seller, or platform admin session context.

relatedAuthLogId.description: Identifier of a related authentication log entry from shopping_mall_auth_logs when this incident is rooted in authentication behavior.

relatedAccessLogId.description: Identifier of a related access log entry from shopping_mall_access_logs when this incident was detected from request/response patterns.

relatedSecurityEventId.description: Identifier of the primary security event record from shopping_mall_security_events that triggered this incident summary.

IShoppingMallSecurityIncidentReport.IReq.description:
Search and filter criteria for retrieving a security incident report for platform administrators.

Encapsulates complex search parameters for querying security incidents aggregated from shopping_mall_security_events, shopping_mall_auth_logs, and shopping_mall_access_logs. Supports time ranges, category and severity filters, actor scoping, infrastructure attributes, and pagination configuration for threat hunting and security monitoring workflows.

from.description: Inclusive start of the time window for incidents to include in the report, expressed as an ISO 8601 UTC date-time string.

to.description: Exclusive end of the time window for incidents to include in the report, expressed as an ISO 8601 UTC date-time string.

categories.description: Optional list of incident categories to include in the report. When omitted, incidents of all categories are considered.

items.description: Incident category string such as authenticationAnomaly, accessPolicyViolation, suspectedFraud, or integrationSecurityIssue.

severities.description: Optional list of severity levels to include, such as info, warning, or critical. When omitted, incidents of all severities are returned.

items.description: Severity level string indicating the importance or criticality of the incident.

principalTypes.description: Optional filter for the types of principals involved in incidents, such as customer, seller, platformAdmin, or guest.

items.description: Principal type string indicating which actor type is associated with the incident.

principalIds.description: Optional list of specific principal identifiers (for example, customer IDs, seller IDs, or platform admin IDs) to constrain the incident search to.

items.description: Identifier of a principal potentially associated with incidents to include in the report.

ipAddresses.description: Optional list of IP addresses to filter incidents by source network location. Useful for correlation and investigation of suspicious origins.

items.description: IP address string, typically IPv4 or IPv6, captured in logging tables.

sessionIds.description: Optional list of session identifiers to filter incidents by authentication or browsing sessions.

items.description: Session identifier string associated with an actor session.

search.description: Free-text search string applied to incident summaries or descriptive fields to quickly locate relevant incidents.

page.description: 1-based page index for pagination of incident results. Defaults to the first page when omitted.

limit.description: Maximum number of incident summaries to return in a single page. Implementations may enforce an upper bound for system safety.

orderBy.description: Field name to sort incidents by, commonly occurredAt or severity.

orderDirection.description: Sort direction for the incidents, either asc for ascending or desc for descending.

IShoppingMallLoggingPerformanceIncident..description:
Search criteria, filters, and pagination parameters for querying performance incident reports from ShoppingMall logging tables.

Represents complex filters over logging-oriented Prisma models such as shopping_mall_error_logs, shopping_mall_access_logs, and shopping_mall_integration_event_logs to retrieve performance-related incidents like slow responses, timeouts, elevated error rates, and similar operational issues.

from.description: Inclusive start of the time window for performance incidents to retrieve, expressed as an ISO 8601 UTC date-time string.

to.description: Exclusive end of the time window for performance incidents to retrieve, expressed as an ISO 8601 UTC date-time string.

incidentTypes.description: Optional list of performance incident types to include in the result, such as slowResponse, timeout, errorSpike, or resourceSaturation.

items.description: Performance incident type string that classifies the type of performance issue.

severities.description: Optional list of severity levels for performance incidents, such as info, warning, or critical.

items.description: Severity level string for performance incidents.

serviceNames.description: Optional list of service or subsystem identifiers to filter incidents to specific parts of the platform.

items.description: Logical service or subsystem name associated with a performance incident.

endpointPaths.description: Optional list of HTTP endpoint paths or route patterns to filter incidents related to specific APIs or web pages.

items.description: HTTP path or route pattern such as /shoppingMall/orders or /shoppingMall/products/*.

minDurationMs.description: Lower bound on request or operation duration in milliseconds used to focus on particularly slow incidents.

maxDurationMs.description: Upper bound on request or operation duration in milliseconds used to limit results to specific latency ranges.

search.description: Free-text search string applied to incident summaries or diagnostic messages.

page.description: 1-based page index for pagination of performance incidents. Defaults to the first page when omitted.

limit.description: Maximum number of performance incident summaries to return in a single page. Implementations may enforce an upper bound for safety.

orderBy.description: Field name to sort performance incidents by, commonly occurredAt, durationMs, or severity.

orderDirection.description: Sort direction for performance incidents, either asc for ascending or desc for descending.

IShoppingMallLoggingIntegrationFailure.I.description:
Search criteria, filters, and pagination parameters for querying integration failure incident reports from ShoppingMall integration event and logging tables.

This DTO is used by platform administrators to filter integration failure logs across external providers such as payment gateways, shipping carriers, notification services, and other third‑party systems. It supports time‑window filtering, provider and integration‑type scoping, failure categorization, severity selection, and pagination/sorting options for analytical dashboards.

page.description:
1‑based page index for paginated result navigation.

Defaults to the first page when omitted. Platform implementations typically cap the maximum page value based on data volume.

limit.description:
Maximum number of incident summaries to return per page.

Backends should enforce an upper bound (for example 50–200) to protect the logging storage from unbounded scans and overly large responses.

from.description:
Start of the time window (inclusive) for filtering integration failures.

Must be an ISO 8601 timestamp. When omitted, the system may use a default look‑back window such as the last 24 or 72 hours.

to.description:
End of the time window (exclusive) for filtering integration failures.

Must be an ISO 8601 timestamp that is not earlier than the `from` value. When omitted, defaults to the current time on the server.

items.description:
Integration type identifier representing a class of external systems.

Examples include `payment_provider`, `shipping_carrier`, `messaging_provider`, `webhook_endpoint`, or other platform‑specific integration categories.

integrationTypes.description:
Filter set of integration types to include in the result.

When provided, only failures from the specified integration type identifiers will be returned.

items.description:
External partner identifier such as a payment gateway code, carrier code, or integration key.

Examples: `stripe`, `paypal`, `fedex`, `internal_notification_bus`.

partnerIdentifiers.description:
List of external partner identifiers to filter on.

If specified, only incidents associated with these partners are included.

oneOf.description:
High‑level failure category for the integration incident.

`timeout` – External system did not respond within configured SLA.
`invalid_response` – Response payload failed validation or parsing.
`authentication_error` – Credentials, tokens, or signatures were rejected.
`throttling` – Rate‑limit or quota enforcement from the external system.
`transport_error` – Network or protocol‑level failure (DNS, TLS, connection reset, etc.).
`internal_mapping_error` – Local mapping, transformation, or routing error prior to or after the external call.
`unknown` – Unclassified or legacy failures.
