Severity level of the error as determined by the application or logging subsystem.

Common values include levels like `info`, `warning`, `error`, and `critical`. In list views and analytics this field is crucial for prioritizing triage and distinguishing high‑impact incidents from low‑severity noise.

message.description:
Primary error message or summarized description of the failure.

The message is intended to be concise and human‑readable for use in list views, dashboards, and quick diagnostics. It may be derived from the original exception message or from a standardized, user‑friendly error description, and should avoid leaking sensitive information.

correlation_id.description:
Correlation or trace identifier used to link this error to a broader workflow or distributed trace.

Operators and developers can use this value to connect error entries with access logs, integration events, and other telemetry records that share the same correlation identifier, enabling end‑to‑end incident analysis.

service_name.description:
Logical name of the service or bounded context that produced the error.

In monolithic deployments this may correspond to a logical module name, while in multi‑service or modular architectures it typically identifies the specific service responsible for the failure. In summaries this field helps localize issues to the appropriate owning team or subsystem.

component_name.description:
Name of the component, module, or subsystem within the service where the error originated.

Examples include domain areas (such as `checkout`, `catalog`, or `fulfillment`) or technical layers (such as `repository`, `integrationAdapter`, or `messageHandler`). This field provides an additional level of granularity beyond `service_name` when analyzing error patterns in grids and dashboards.

created_at.description:
Timestamp when this error event was recorded by the backend.

The value is stored as a `DateTime` column in the `shopping_mall_error_logs` table and reflects the time at which the failure was observed. In summary and analytics views it is used for sorting, time‑range filtering, and correlation with access, integration, and security logs.

IShoppingMallIntegrationEventLog.ISummar.description:
Lightweight summary view of an integration event log entry used for list and dashboard responses.

This summary DTO is also annotated with `x-autobe-prisma-schema: shopping_mall_integration_event_logs`, so every field directly maps to a real column on the underlying Prisma model. It intentionally focuses on identifiers, provider classification, status, latency, HTTP code, and key error and correlation information so that operators can quickly scan integration health without loading full payload snippets for every row.

id.description:
Primary key of the integration event log record, taken from the `id` column.

Used by list UIs and monitoring tools to link each summary row to its corresponding detail view or to other log streams that reference integration events by ID.

provider_type.description:
High-level provider category stored in the `provider_type` column, such as `payment`, `email`, or `shipping`.

List and dashboard screens commonly group or filter by this field to focus on specific integration domains when investigating incidents.

provider_name.description:
Concrete provider name or identifier for this event, from the `provider_name` column.

It allows operators to quickly see which gateway, carrier, or external system is responsible for each log entry when scanning summaries.

event_type.description:
Type of integration event stored in the `event_type` column, such as a specific request or notification type.

Displayed in summary lists so that administrators can distinguish between different kinds of integration activity at a glance.

direction.description:
Direction of the integration event relative to the platform, taken from the `direction` column.

Summaries surface this field so that observers can immediately see whether an entry represents an outbound call or an inbound callback or webhook.

request_id.description:
Platform-level request correlation identifier stored in the `request_id` column of the `shopping_mall_integration_event_logs` table.

This value links a particular integration event back to a broader application request or workflow, allowing operators and developers to correlate integration behaviour with access logs, error logs, and tracing spans directly from summary views.

provider_request_id.description:
External provider request identifier stored in the `provider_request_id` column.

When present, this field contains the request ID or reference generated by the external system for the outbound call. It is included in the summary DTO so that support teams can quickly copy or filter by the provider-side request reference without opening the full detail record.

provider_response_id.description:
External provider response or transaction identifier stored in the `provider_response_id` column.

For providers that distinguish between request and response identifiers, this value makes it easy to correlate the platform’s log entry with provider-side transaction records or support tickets when scanning list or dashboard views.

status.description:
Overall status of the integration event, from the `status` column.

This field is crucial in list views to highlight failures or timeouts among large volumes of successful events and to drive high-level error-rate indicators.

correlation_id.description:
Correlation identifier stored in the `correlation_id` column, used to tie this integration event to broader workflows or entities.

It is included in summary responses so that operators can copy or filter by correlation ID directly from list views without opening detailed records.

http_status_code.description:
HTTP status code recorded in the `http_status_code` column for HTTP-based outbound calls.

Summaries often display this alongside `status` to distinguish between client errors, server errors, and successful responses when scanning many events quickly.

latency_ms.description:
Latency in milliseconds stored in the `latency_ms` column describing how long the external provider took to respond.

Exposed in summaries to help spot slow or timing-out integrations and to feed aggregated performance visualizations without fetching full detail records.

error_code.description:
Machine-readable error code from the `error_code` column, populated when the integration event is not successful.

This field allows list views to surface succinct error identifiers that can be used for filtering, alert routing, or linking to runbooks.

error_message.description:
Human-readable error message from the `error_message` column associated with the integration event.

In summaries this may be truncated by the UI layer, but including it in the DTO allows administrators to get a quick sense of what went wrong without always opening the full detail endpoint.

created_at.description:
Creation timestamp of the integration event log record, taken from the `created_at` column.

Used as the primary time axis in list responses and analytics widgets so operators can order and filter integration events in chronological order.

IShoppingMallLoggingPerformanceIncident..description:
Summary representation of a performance-related incident detected by the shopping mall logging and monitoring subsystem.

Used primarily in admin dashboards, alerts, and correlation views where operators need to quickly understand which component, endpoint, or integration is experiencing latency, error-rate spikes, or other performance problems without loading full incident detail payloads.

id.description: Unique identifier of the performance incident record.

detected_at.description:
Timestamp when the monitoring system detected or first registered the performance incident.

Expressed in ISO 8601 date-time format with timezone information.

severity.description:
Severity level of the incident as classified by the monitoring system.

Typical values include `info`, `warning`, `minor`, `major`, `critical`. Implementations may define stricter enums in code to match alerting policies.

category.description:
High-level performance category describing the nature of the incident.

Examples: `latency`, `error-rate`, `throughput`, `saturation`, `resource-exhaustion`.

This field is used to group incidents in dashboards and to drive routing to the appropriate on-call teams.

source_type.description:
Type of source that generated or is affected by the incident.

Typical examples: `api-endpoint`, `background-job`, `integration`, `database`, `cache`, `queue`.

This field is useful to narrow down which subsystem is degraded.

source_identifier.description:
Identifier of the affected source within the specified source type.

For example, an API route path (`/orders/{orderId}`), job name (`recalculate-seller-metrics`), integration key (`payment-gateway:stripe`), or database query group name.

metric_name.description:
Name of the primary metric that triggered the incident.

Examples: `p95_latency_ms`, `error_rate`, `throughput_rps`, `queue_lag_seconds`, `cpu_usage_percent`.

current_value.description:
Current measured value of the primary metric at the time the incident was detected.

For latency metrics this is typically milliseconds; for error rates usually a fraction or percentage; for throughput a rate per second or minute.

threshold_value.description:
Configured threshold value that the metric exceeded (or fell below) to trigger the incident.

This allows operators to see how far out of bounds the metric is and supports SLA/SLO analysis.

unit.description:
Measurement unit of the metric values.

Examples: `ms`, `seconds`, `percent`, `rps`, `ops`, `count`, `bytes`. This field is intended for display in dashboards and reports.

status.description:
Current lifecycle status of the incident.

Examples: `open`, `acknowledged`, `mitigated`, `resolved`, `closed`. Implementations may enforce a stricter enum and workflow at the service level.

correlation_id.description:
Correlation identifier shared with other logs and traces that are related to this incident, such as integration events, access logs, or error logs.

Typically a trace ID, request ID, or an incident group key used for cross-system observability.

IShoppingMallLoggingIntegrationFailure.I.description:
Summary view of a failed integration event within the shopping mall platform.

Provides a lightweight snapshot of an integration failure log entry that is suitable for list views, monitoring dashboards, and cross-linking from other entities. This summary focuses on identifiers, high‑level context about the failing integration, and minimal diagnostic information needed to triage or drill down into detailed logs.

Typical use cases include: displaying recent failures in an admin console, aggregating failures per integration provider, or linking to a detailed failure record for in‑depth analysis.

id.description:
Unique identifier of the integration failure log entry.

This UUID is generated by the system when the failure is recorded and is used as the primary reference when drilling down to a detailed view or correlating with other logs.

occurred_at.description:
Timestamp when the integration failure occurred in ISO 8601 date-time format.

Represents the moment the platform detected or recorded the failure, not when it is later processed or viewed.

provider.description:
Logical name or identifier of the external integration provider or subsystem where the failure occurred.

Examples include names of payment gateways, messaging providers, logistics APIs, or internal microservices that the shopping mall platform depends on.

integration_type.description:
High‑level classification of the type of integration operation that failed.

Common examples might include values such as `payment_webhook`, `shipment_update`, `refund_notification`, or `catalog_sync`. This field is intended for reporting, filtering, and routing but is not restricted to a fixed enumeration at the schema level.

status_code.description:
Status or error code associated with the integration failure when available.

For HTTP-based integrations, this is typically the HTTP status code returned by the external service. For non‑HTTP integrations, this may represent a domain‑specific numeric error code.

error_code.description:
Optional short machine‑readable error code that categorizes the reason for the failure.

This value is usually derived from the external provider’s response or from internal validation logic. It is suitable for grouping, analytics, and conditional handling in monitoring tools.

error_message.description:
Human‑readable message describing the integration failure in concise terms.

Intended to give operators enough context to understand what went wrong without needing to open the full detailed log record. For example, it may summarize validation errors, timeout conditions, or authentication problems.

correlation_id.description:
Correlation identifier used to link this integration failure with related requests, background jobs, or trace spans.

This field allows cross‑system tracing, making it easier to follow a single logical transaction across multiple services, logs, and monitoring systems.

retryable.description:
Indicates whether this integration failure is considered retryable under current business rules.

A value of `true` means that automated retry logic or manual re‑execution is allowed or recommended. A value of `false` typically indicates permanent failures such as invalid configuration, permission issues, or data contract mismatches.

IShoppingMallAuthCredentialsActor.ISumma.description:
Polymorphic summary view of the actor that owns a given authentication credential.

This helper DTO wraps the BELONGS-TO association from `shopping_mall_auth_credentials` to the concrete actor tables (customer, seller, platform administrator). It uses the universal `.ISummary` pattern for each actor type and is designed to be embedded in `IShoppingMallAuthCredentials.ISummary` so that admin and security tools can see who a credential belongs to in a single list response.

Only one of the actor-specific summary properties (customer, seller, platformAdmin) will be non-null for a given instance, depending on the `actorType` discriminator. This keeps the structure explicit while remaining type-safe for code generation.

actorType.description:
Discriminator indicating which concrete actor type owns the credential.

This value aligns with the `actor_type` column on `shopping_mall_auth_credentials` and determines which of the actor summary properties (customer, seller, platformAdmin) is populated.

Only the following literal values are valid here, and client and server implementations MUST treat this field as an enum-like discriminator:
- `customer`  → `customer` summary is populated
- `seller`    → `seller` summary is populated
- `platformadmin` → `platformAdmin` summary is populated.

Any other value must be rejected during validation or mapped to an explicit error in API implementations.

customer.description:
Summary of the customer account that owns the credential when `actorType` is `customer`.

This property is null or omitted for non-customer credentials. It uses the customer `.ISummary` projection to avoid deep nesting while providing enough information for admin and security UIs.

seller.description:
Summary of the seller account that owns the credential when `actorType` is `seller`.

This property is null or omitted for non-seller credentials. It uses the seller `.ISummary` projection, giving lightweight context about the merchant associated with the credential.

platformAdmin.description:
Summary of the platform administrator account that owns the credential when `actorType` is `platformadmin`.

This property is null or omitted for credentials belonging to other actor types. It uses the platform administrator `.ISummary` projection so that security tooling can easily identify the owner of highly privileged credentials.

IShoppingMallSecurityEventMetadata.description:
Container object for arbitrary structured metadata associated with a single security event in the shoppingMall platform.

This object behaves as a flexible key–value map whose entries carry implementation-specific diagnostic or correlation data, such as rule identifiers, geolocation hints, correlation IDs, or risk scoring details.

Each entry value is represented by IShoppingMallSecurityEventMetadataValue, allowing security and risk components to attach arbitrarily structured JSON payloads while keeping the top-level IShoppingMallSecurityEvent contract stable for administrative APIs.

additionalProperties.description:
Dynamically keyed metadata entry associated with the security event.

Each property name on the `IShoppingMallSecurityEventMetadata` object represents a logical metadata field such as `rule_id`, `geo_location`, `correlation_id`, or `risk_score`. The corresponding value is an `IShoppingMallSecurityEventMetadataValue` instance that encapsulates an arbitrary JSON object payload describing that aspect in more detail.

Security, risk, and observability subsystems are expected to define and document the concrete keys they emit (for example, which rule IDs or device-fingerprint structures are used), while API consumers should treat unknown keys as opaque but safely ignorable metadata. This design keeps the metadata channel extensible without requiring breaking changes to the core security event schema.

IShoppingMallSecurityEventMetadataValue.description:
Single metadata value object stored within the IShoppingMallSecurityEventMetadata map.

This type models a free-form JSON object that can contain nested fields describing rule evaluation details, device fingerprints, enrichment payloads, or other diagnostic structures provided by security and risk subsystems.

Consumers of administrative security APIs should treat instances of this type as opaque, implementation-defined structures and rely on separate documentation or naming conventions to interpret particular metadata keys and shapes.

Use this when the metadata entry is best represented as plain text, such as identifiers, textual status labels, or short serialized codes emitted by security and risk subsystems.

Use this for scores, numeric identifiers, counters, or other quantitative measures produced by security and risk evaluation pipelines.

Arbitrary boolean metadata value.

Use this for simple flags such as whether a particular rule fired, whether a condition was met, or whether a specific security attribute is present.

IShoppingMallProductSkuChannelVisibility.description:
Per-channel visibility overrides for a product SKU in update operations.

Represents boolean switches that allow the caller to explicitly enable or disable visibility of a SKU on specific sales channels such as the primary web storefront, mobile experiences, or external marketplaces.

These flags are evaluated in combination with higher-level activation fields like `isActive` and `isPurchasable` to compute final catalog exposure for the SKU.

web.description:
Whether this SKU is visible on the primary web storefront channel.

When set to false, the SKU is hidden from web catalog listings and product detail pages even if it is active and purchasable in general.

mobile.description:
Whether this SKU is visible on mobile applications or mobile-specific storefronts.

This flag can be used to run staged rollouts or channel-specific merchandising strategies on mobile.

marketplace.description:
Whether this SKU is visible on external or third-party marketplace integrations handled by the platform.

Disabling this flag keeps the SKU internal to the core storefront while preventing synchronization to connected marketplaces.

IShoppingMallProductSkuMetadata.IUpdate.description:
Free-form metadata container for SKU-level custom attributes in update operations.

Represents a flexible key-value map that allows integrators and downstream systems to attach additional non-modeled attributes to a SKU, such as external system identifiers, feature flags, or analytics tags.

Each entry is stored as a string value so that arbitrary metadata can be safely transported without enforcing a rigid schema, while still keeping the overall structure in a named, reusable type.

additionalProperties.description:
A single metadata value associated with a custom key.

Metadata values are stored as strings so callers can serialize booleans, numbers, or JSON themselves if needed, while the backend treats them as opaque text.

IShoppingMallOrderReturnRequestItem.ISum.description:
Summary representation of a single line item that participates in an order return request.

Each instance describes the linkage to a specific order line in `shopping_mall_order_lines` and the quantity from that line that is included in the return request. It is designed for embedding inside `IShoppingMallOrderReturnRequest` and related views without requiring an additional API call to inspect the per-line breakdown.

order_line_id.description:
Identifier of the order line in the `shopping_mall_order_lines` table that this return entry refers to.

The parent order referenced by the `order` property on `IShoppingMallOrderReturnRequest` contains the authoritative pricing and fulfillment snapshot for this line.

quantity.description:
Number of units from the referenced order line that are included in this return request.

The value is always greater than or equal to one and is constrained by the maximum number of units that have been delivered and not previously returned for the same order line.

IShoppingMallOrderReturnRequestAttachmen.description:
Summary representation of a single evidence attachment associated with an order return request.

Attachments are compositional children of the return request and typically reference immutable media such as photos or documents that help reviewers evaluate the claim. This summary type is used when embedding attachments into `IShoppingMallOrderReturnRequest` and related DTOs.

The shopping mall platform follows a strict URL-only file handling model. Backend APIs never accept or return raw binary or base64-encoded file content; instead, they only work with pre-uploaded file URLs that are managed by a dedicated storage layer.

name.description:
Human-readable name or caption for this evidence attachment, suitable for display in customer and back-office UIs.

Clients typically derive this from the original file name or from a user-provided caption at upload time. The value should be concise but descriptive enough to help reviewers understand what the attachment shows without opening it.

extension.description:
File extension of the evidence resource, such as `jpg`, `png`, or `pdf`.

This value is used for basic client-side rendering decisions and for simple validation of attachment types. It should reflect the actual file type stored at the `url`, without a leading dot and using lowercase by convention.

url.description:
Public or signed URL pointing to the immutable, already-uploaded file associated with this evidence attachment.

Clients must upload the binary asset to a storage service first and then supply only this reference URL to the shopping mall backend. The backend never accepts binary data or base64 content in this field; it treats the URL as an opaque pointer that can be dereferenced by clients when they need to view the evidence.

type.description:
Optional business classification of the attachment within the context of the return request, such as `product_photo`, `package_photo`, or `receipt`.

The precise set of values is determined by platform configuration. When omitted, the consumer may infer the role of the attachment from its usage context or MIME type, but clients are encouraged to populate this field to improve review efficiency and downstream analytics.

IShoppingMallPaymentAuthorizationRiskMet.description:
Wrapper type for risk or fraud-related metadata associated with a payment authorization attempt.

Instances of this schema are stored alongside authorization records to capture auxiliary information from fraud engines, rule evaluators, or external payment providers, such as risk scores, rule identifiers, device fingerprints, or behavioral indicators.

The structure of the JSON document is intentionally flexible and may evolve over time according to the needs of risk analysis components, so no fixed set of typed properties is enforced at the schema level. Implementations should treat this object as an opaque JSON blob and rely on higher-level contracts or documentation to interpret its contents.

oneOf.description:
String-valued risk metadata entry.

Typical examples include rule identifiers, textual reason codes, device or session identifiers, geographic codes, or provider-specific status strings. Use this type for values that are inherently textual or where downstream systems expect human-readable labels.

Numeric risk metadata entry.

Use this for scalar metrics such as risk scores, probability values, transaction amount normalizations, or counters returned by fraud engines or payment providers.

Boolean risk metadata entry.

Use this for flag-like fields, such as `is_high_risk`, `device_trusted`, or `velocity_check_passed`, where the metadata represents a simple true/false indicator.

Explicit null risk metadata value.

This can be used when a key is known in the contract but intentionally carries no value for a particular authorization attempt, allowing consumers to distinguish between missing keys and keys that are present but empty.
